title: What each transitivity screen can see
question: Do the available transitivity screens (covariate dissimilarity, loop inconsistency, heterogeneity), run together, detect the violations that bias a network estimate, and can their pattern of flags identify the mechanism?
design: Triangle networks with two or five studies per comparison and five violation mechanisms, including a loop-consistent unmeasured modifier constructed to be invisible to every screen; 26 cells, 2000 replicates each; detection, bias, coverage and mechanism identification.
answer: No. Each screen sees one direction of violation, and an unmeasured modifier that makes one treatment look better in every comparison that includes it is invisible to all three: at size 0.4 it biased the network estimate by 0.40 with coverage near zero while the screens together fired at their null rate (0.28). Loop breaks and drift were detected with power rising in the number of studies, but the pattern of flags identified the mechanism poorly, and a measured modifier was always flagged although adjustment removed its bias.
findings: Refuting sentence fails: loop-consistent unmeasured modification of 0.4, any-screen detection 0.281 and 0.279 against 0.274 and 0.283 with no violation; bias -0.40.
Loop break of 0.4: detected in 0.77 (2 studies per comparison) and 0.98 (5); drift of 0.4: 0.95 and 1.00.
Measured modifier: dissimilarity flagged 100% of analyses; meta-regression bias at most 0.003.
Mechanism read from the flag pattern: loop breaks 43% correct, drift 34%; drift often triggered the loop test.
not_answered: Stylized triangle networks with continuous estimates; calendar drift as random shifts; abandonment records not scored. Peer review has not been done.
estimand: B versus C effect in a declared target population
